item.title: Sporadic gunfire sends Ethiopians fleeing into Kenya as trucks remain stuck at border
item.description:
Sporadic gunfire sends Ethiopians fleeing into Kenya as trucks remain stuck at border
Gunfire was heard from the Ethiopian border town of Moyale as civilians continue to flee into Kenya to escape violence from a regional disputeByANDREW KASUKU Associated Press and KHALED KAZZIHA Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 6:21 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MOYALE, Kenya -- Sporadic gunfire could be heard coming from the Ethiopian border town of Moyale on Friday as Ethiopian civilians continued fleeing into Kenya to escape violence stemming from a regional dispute.
Cargo trucks were stranded on both sides of the border as tensions persisted between leaders of the Oromia and Somali regional states of Ethiopia.
An Associated Press reporter in Moyale, Kenya, recorded gunfire coming from the Ethiopian side of the border and reported hearing sporadic gunfire daily since Oct. 22.
Up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya, the U.N. refugee agency said Wednesday, citing local authorities, up from 36,000 reported Tuesday. Registration and verification were continuing, the agency said.
Benedict Munywoki, deputy county commissioner for Moyale Sub-County, said Thursday that some of those fleeing Ethiopia were staying in town rather than in camps, making an accurate count difficult.
“The initial number of people who are in camps and also integrated into the community is still growing day by day,” he said.
The U.N. refugee agency, the International Organization for Migration and the Kenya Red Cross were working to provide medical care, food and shelter.
At a camp established by the Kenya Red Cross, people cooked food in large pots over wood fires Thursday while health workers weighed children and measured their upper arms to check for malnutrition.
Seifu Negash, an Ethiopian doctor who fled into Kenya, was volunteering with the Kenya Red Cross to treat fellow refugees.

item.title: Brief truce agreed by Russia and Ukraine allows aid operation in Oleshky
item.description:
Brief truce agreed by Russia and Ukraine allows aid operation in Oleshky
Russian and Ukrainian officials have entered the devastated city of Oleshky following a rare ceasefire brokered by U.S. first lady Melania TrumpByHANNA ARHIROVA Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 4:04 AM
KHERSON, Ukraine -- A humanitarian mission entered the devastated city of Oleshky on Friday, officials said, as Russia and Ukraine observed the most significant truce of the 4½-year war that began with Moscow’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
A convoy including 25 buses, ambulances and aid supplies was due to arrive in the Russian-occupied city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate residents wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine. About 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to authorities and volunteers.
A localized ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has held for four days and is due to continue through Sunday evening to allow the operation to proceed.
“Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will have the opportunity to do so safely,” Russia and Ukraine said in identical statements. “Those who choose to stay may remain and will receive all the humanitarian support they need.”
Officials from both countries worked together in a rare joint humanitarian effort, offering a brief bright spot in a grim war of attrition.
The United States played a central role in the mission, which the White House said was brokered by first lady Melania Trump. Pope Leo XIV also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to help Oleshky.
Fighting continued elsewhere, however. Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched ballistic and other missiles, along with scores of drones.
The convoy assembled in Armiansk, a town in Russian-occupied Ukraine about 85 kilometers (53 miles) south of Oleshky, said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman and chief negotiator.

item.title: Evacuees reunite with family at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border after fleeing Oleshky
item.description:
Evacuees reunite with family at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border after fleeing Oleshky
Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have crossed into Ukrainian-held territoryByDEREK GATOPOULOS Associated Press and EFREM LUKATSKY Associated PressOctober 31, 2026, 5:39 AM
Share
CHERNIHIV REGION, Ukraine -- Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory Saturday in a major rescue operation carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine 4½ years ago.
Evacuees wrapped in blue and yellow Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border and reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed out coffee to the weary travelers who had traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the convoy.
Tetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee.
“We love them, we love them,” she said through tears. “We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud.”
The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began early Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House has said U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the localized deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia and Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and evacuations.
Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.
Holding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky.

item.title: At a new Amsterdam museum, humans are caged as dead animals hang and roam around them
item.description:
At a new Amsterdam museum, humans are caged as dead animals hang and roam around them
Amsterdam's new Art Zoo museum offers a unique experience with its eclectic collection of preserved creatures and artful displaysByMOLLY QUELL Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 1:46 AM
AMSTERDAM -- Look up as you enter Amsterdam's new Art Zoo museum, and a 12-foot crocodile stares down at you, mouth open, ready to chomp.
The taxidermic reptile is one of hundreds of preserved creatures on display, alongside artfully arranged piles of bones, illuminated tulips encased in apothecary jars and a cabinet of grotesque fish.
While it’s not a Halloween-themed museum, the show should appeal to anybody looking for something a little dark this spooky season.
“It was a little creepy,” admitted Tomáš Vaško, a Slovak living in the Dutch capital, after touring the museum on a dark October day.
Art Zoo is the creation of Dutch artists Jaap Sinke and Ferry van Tongeren, who draw inspiration from “wunderkammers,” or curiosity cabinets collected by wealthy Europeans in the 16th and 17th centuries to showcase objects from the natural world.
“The main thing is that we like storytelling with the animals," van Tongeren told The Associated Press. "We like to add drama. We add an attitude to the animals, where traditional taxidermists just want to mimic nature.”
Behind him, a cheetah slouched in an alcove under the watchful eye of a cassowary.
In natural history museums, animals are posed as they could be seen in the wild. At the Art Zoo, a Japanese giant spider crab stretches its 6-foot legs above a doorway beside the leg bones of a mastodon that nearly reaches the ceiling.
The duo rose to fame in 2015 after shark-pickling artist Damien Hirst purchased their entire exhibition from a London art show.

item.title: Cuba welcomes home diplomat expelled from US after unusual altercation at the UN
item.description:
Cuba welcomes home diplomat expelled from US after unusual altercation at the UN
Cuba has welcomed home a diplomat expelled by the United States after a heated confrontation at the United Nations this weekByANDREA RODRÍGUEZ Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 1:07 PM
Share
HAVANA -- HAVANA (AP) — Cuba on Friday welcomed home a diplomat expelled by the United States after an unusually heated confrontation between the two countries’ representatives at the United Nations this week.
Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Gerardo Peñalver posted a photo of Richard Tur de la Concepción, first secretary of Cuba’s U.N. mission, alongside Foreign Ministry officials holding a Cuban flag at Havana’s airport. It was Cuba’s first public response since the U.S. State Department announced it would take action against Tur after he tried to knock a phone out of a U.S. diplomat’s hand.
“We welcomed the young diplomat home,” Peñalver wrote on X, saying Tur had “firmly and with dignity confronted the disrespectful and provocative behavior” of the U.S. delegation.
Peñalver accused U.S. officials of trying to disrupt a vote on a resolution condemning the U.S. embargo on Cuba and undermine Tur’s candidacy for a position on a U.N. body.
Tur’s expulsion was announced by U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz and later confirmed by the U.S. State Department.
U.S. officials accused Tur of shoving an American diplomat and trying to snatch the phone he was using to record their confrontation Tuesday during a General Assembly session on the embargo.
The encounter escalated into a shouting match between Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez.
Cuba said Tur was defending himself after his personal space was invaded.

item.title: UK PM signals the government will consider an apology for its role in the slave trade
item.description:
UK PM signals the government will consider an apology for its role in the slave trade
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham says his government will consider apologizing for the first time for its role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade as it seeks to strengthen relations with nations in Africa and the CaribbeanByDANICA KIRKA Associated PressOctober 31, 2026, 5:48 AM
LONDON -- U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham says his government will consider apologizing for the first time for its role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade as it seeks to strengthen relations with nations in Africa and the Caribbean.
Writing in the Guardian on Saturday, Burnham said Britain needed to acknowledge its “complicated history” in order to protect the Commonwealth, an association of 56 independent nations that grew out of the British Empire. Burnham travels to Antigua and Barbuda next week for a meeting of Commonwealth leaders.
“For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery,” Burnham said. “By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.”
Burnham said his government is offering to begin a “structured dialogue” with those affected by slavery and will listen to calls for a formal apology by the British state. But he said Britain would continue to resist calls for it to pay reparations for the slave trade.
“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” Burnham said.
Instead, the prime minister said he wanted to address the issues that face the Commonwealth and other nations today, including high levels of debt faced by many developing countries.
Burnham said he would work with other wealthy nations and investors to help vulnerable countries pay off their debts over a longer period and at lower interest rat...

item.title: In Afghanistan, musicians defy music ban to keep traditions alive
item.description:
In Afghanistan, musicians defy music ban to keep traditions alive
Music has been banned in Afghanistan for five years, with the ruling Taliban only allowing religious tunesByELENA BECATOROS Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 1:03 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KABUL, Afghanistan -- There was a time when music would fill many of Kabul’s streets, wafting out of cafes and restaurants, seeping out of homes in the warren of alleys that make up the Afghan capital’s music district.
Those days are long gone.
Since 2022, playing or listening to music has been officially banned throughout Afghanistan. The Taliban who seized power in 2021 have prohibited anything but religious music — unaccompanied vocal chanting — with the ban enforced by the feared morality police of the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice.
“Music is forbidden in Islam,” said ministry spokesperson Saif ul Islam Khyber, adding that it “serves as a means of joy to Satan,” and that it “often leads to various other vices.” No one, he said, "is permitted to listen to music or to record songs and musical compositions.”
Many musicians and performers fled the country after the takeover. Those who remained sent their instruments abroad or hid them to save them from being smashed by authorities.
The music shops in Kucha-e-Kharabat, the neighborhood in Kabul's old city where many musicians lived, now sell other wares, from food and groceries to clothes and household goods. Anything except musical instruments.
Across Afghanistan, musicians lost their livelihoods overnight.
Yet for many, music is in their blood. It has flowed through their families for generations, and the thought of never playing again is unbearable. Every so often, some pull out their instruments and play in secret. A knock at the door could mean danger. Still, they play.

item.title: Spain train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
item.description:
Spain train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blameByJOSEPH WILSON Associated Press and IAIN SULLIVAN Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 1:03 AM
Share
URDA, Spain -- Was Spain's second major train collision this year caused by human error or does it show severe cracks in its once touted high-speed rail network?
Spain’s transport minister has laid most of the blame on a traffic controller’s poor judgment for Wednesday's collision in Toledo province, which killed 69 people.
But railway unions have pushed back. They point to what they describe as deteriorating working conditions — fewer traffic controllers with more work than ever — that have made it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of millions of passengers.
While the country searched for answers, police with sniffer dogs were still sifting through the wreckage on Friday. Regional authorities didn’t rule out that the death toll could still rise.
This was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, over two hours farther south, one train jumped the track and hit another going in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash is still under investigation.
“It is unacceptable that a country like Spain with such a strong high-speed railway has two accidents of this type in the same year,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Friday from the crash site near the town of Urda.
Spain’s high-speed rail network has been considered a success of state industrial policy. It is the world’s second-largest, after China’s. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.

item.title: Police probe into ex-Prince Andrew and Epstein's visit to king's estate
item.description:
Police probe into ex-Prince Andrew and Epstein's visit to king's estate
Police in Scotland are investigating former Prince Andrew's time at the king's estate at Balmoral with Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine MaxwellByThe Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 6:17 AM
Share
LONDON -- Police in Scotland are conducting inquiries into the time former Prince Andrew spent at the king’s private estate at Balmoral with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, authorities said Friday.
Police Scotland said the inquiries were at a "very early stage.''
“All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries,'' police said in a statement. “We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”
Images released earlier this year by the U.S. Department of Justice appeared to show the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, on a shooting trip at the estate with Epstein.

item.title: Russia's top independent newspaper shuts down, blaming pressure from authorities
item.description:
Russia's top independent newspaper shuts down, blaming pressure from authorities
Russia's renowned independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, has announced its closure after over three decades, citing relentless official pressureByThe Associated PressOctober 30, 2026, 10:00 AM
MOSCOW -- Russia's most renowned independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, on Friday announced its closure after more than three decades of operation, blaming relentless official pressure.
“They have killed us,” it said in an editorial statement, announcing that it will shut its office on Nov. 9 after publishing its final issue. “The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease operations.”
There was no immediate comment from Russian authorities.
Novaya Gazeta was launched in 1993 with assistance from former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, who used part of his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize to fund it. It was Russia's last major independent media outlet critical of the Kremlin after others either shut or had their websites blocked after President Vladimir Putin sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022.
The paper has been the subject of a sweeping crackdown on dissent that has intensified after the start of the conflict in Ukraine. Authorities have methodically targeted people and organizations critical of the Kremlin, branding many “foreign agents” and declaring some “undesirable” under a law that made membership in “undesirable” organizations a criminal offense.
Novaya Gazeta long has been a thorn in the Kremlin’s side. Six of its journalists were killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War at the start of Putin’s first term as Russian president. She was shot dead in her apartment building in 2006.
Five men were convicted of involvement in her murder in 2014, but there has never been a ruling on who ordered her killing.
